acceptance.output_evidence:
RECORDED FOR L9, NO VERDICT.

1. FAILURE MODES THE SEVEN ARMS DO NOT COVER. (i) A KMS KEY DISABLED. None of the seven arms touches key state (aws_kms_key.irpt, core/kms.tf) -- a disabled or scheduled-for-deletion system CMK would make EVERY table read, EVERY S3 GetObject on an encrypted object, and EVERY queue receive fail simultaneously across ALL firms at once, which is the opposite of the per-tenant isolation these arms exist to prove; no arm here exercises that path or a recovery from it. (ii) A BUCKET POLICY EDITED BY HAND. Every arm here runs application-level logic (a Python read/write through boto3 under this cell's own or a fixture's IAM identity); none of them edits, or recovers from an edit to, a bucket policy or an IAM policy document outside Terraform. A hand-edit that widened or narrowed a firm's S3 prefix grant would not be caught by any of the seven -- it would only be caught by re-applying Terraform (drift detection) or by comp-iam's GRANTED-plane read, neither of which this battery runs. (iii) A GRAPH DELTA THAT NEVER EXPIRES. Arm (c) (duplicated_event) exercises a delta feed that RE-SERVES an old page (a resync); it does not exercise a delta cursor that Microsoft Graph considers PERMANENTLY VALID (never issuing a 410 Gone / resyncRequired) while the underlying mailbox has moved on structurally -- that failure mode belongs to IB-s-6's own poller/checkpoint tests (a live Graph behavior this project has no recorded specimen of, per intake/ib_s_6_graph_inspection.md), not to this cell's arms.

2. WHETHER 'NO PATH BY WHICH A SECOND FIRM COULD BE TOUCHED' IS SHOWN BY THE ARMS OR ONLY BY THE IAM CONDITIONS -- NAMED. BOTH, but on DIFFERENT AXES, and neither alone is the whole claim. The ARMS show it EMPIRICALLY at the DATA-LAYER for the seven scenarios actually driven: a second firm's real QA S3 objects hash byte-identical before and after each arm (28 of 28 total object-hash comparisons across all seven arms, 4 of 4 per arm). That is evidence about WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENED for these seven code paths, on this run, against this data -- it is not evidence that NO code path in this cell COULD reach a second firm, because six of the seven arms make no S3 call at all (offline fixtures), so their second-firm hash pairs are trivially unchanged rather than a structural proof of anything. The IAM CONDITIONS (infra/aws/terraform/investor-reporting/core/iam_firm_conditions.tf, IB-s-5; this cell's own ops/iam.tf) show it STRUCTURALLY: irpt-status-role's policy is prefix-scoped per firm bucket for the directory read and table-scoped (not partition-scoped, since these three DynamoDB tables are keyed by tenant/source as their OWN partition key -- a caller with GetItem/Query on the table can in principle address ANY tenant's partition; the CROSS-FIRM BOUNDARY on those three tables is enforced by the APPLICATION reading only ITS OWN resolved tenant's key, not by a DynamoDB-level condition, because these are shared PAY_PER_REQUEST tables by IB-s-17's own design, not per-firm tables). So: S3 cross-firm isolation is BOTH shown empirically (this cell's arms) AND structurally (S3 prefix conditions); DynamoDB cross-firm isolation is NOT enforced by an IAM condition at all in this cell's role -- it depends on status.py's own code always keying by the caller's resolved tenant, which is a CODE-LEVEL invariant this proof instance asserts but the IAM plane cannot verify on its own. This is worth stating plainly rather than folding into the arms' own gate: the token IBS16-RECOVERY-ISOLATED being printed proves the SEVEN SCENARIOS DRIVEN were isolated; it does not prove DynamoDB-level cross-firm isolation is IAM-enforced, because it is not.

3. WHAT THE RUNBOOK ASSUMES ABOUT THE OPERATOR'S OWN PERMISSIONS. RUNBOOK.md states explicitly (and this cell verified against core/roles.tf and ops/iam.tf) that an operator CANNOT assume any of this project's execution_roles (trust policy admits lambda.amazonaws.com only). The runbook's own recovery steps assume the operator instead has: lambda:InvokeFunction on the four named functions (invoking under the OPERATOR's own identity, with the function then running under ITS OWN execution role); read access to the QA S3 prefixes and to irpt-jobs/irpt-checkpoints/irpt-requests for diagnosis; and access to the guarded irpt-status endpoint itself via an admin-role session (not a service credential). The runbook does NOT assume, and explicitly refuses to offer a procedure requiring, direct DynamoDB PutItem/UpdateItem or S3 write on a served prefix by the operator -- every recovery path in it is 're-invoke the job', never 'hand-edit the state'. This is a STATED assumption, not a verified one: this cell did not apply or test an actual OPERATOR IAM identity (no such role exists in this project today), so the runbook's permission list is a DESIGN ASSERTION about what an operator role SHOULD grant, not a measured read of one that exists.
